newsitem.title: IRAN: Khatami voters jubilant after Iran election win.
newsitem.headline: Khatami voters jubilant after Iran election win.

text.p: Supporters of moderate Mohammad Khatami were jubilant on Saturday as news spread that the former culture minister had clinched a stunning landslide victory in Iran's presidential election.

Iran's Interior Ministry said Khatami had secured 11,713,679 votes or nearly two-thirds of the total 17,644,586 counted by 1130 GMT, versus 4,964,886 votes for his nearest rival, conservative parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who had been strongly tipped to win.
The size of the turnout was expected to be the biggest since the country voted to become an Islamic republic in 1979.
Khatami's victory had been helped by his appeal as a moderate and social reformer, particularly to Iranian women and the country's large young population, analysts said.

"I am very happy. It was very important that Nateq-Nouri did not become president. For the first time the people have rejected what the establishment wanted," said Mitra, a 20-year-old woman student in one of Tehran's main shopping streets.
More social freedom for young people and women became a central issue of the campaign, together with problems of rampant inflation and unemployment.

"The important thing is that people have voted for someone who attaches importance to civil liberties which have not existed before," said Mori, a 30-year-old man who was listening to a radio in a tailor's shop in central Tehran.
"The government will gradually go towards liberalisation. You can't expect democracy but we hope that people in the future can be more relaxed," he said with a smile.

Some shopowners were handing out boxes of sweet cakes to friends and customers in celebration as news came through on state-run radio that Nateq-Nouri had sent a message congratulating Khatami for his election success.
"My heart is thrilled. In my neighbourhood I went to every door asking them to vote for Khatami," said Abolfath, a 65-year-old car park attendant.

"The welfare of the young people will improve, our economy and international relations will also improve...some of the restrictions that existed will be wiped out," said Babak, a 30- year-old computer salesman in the capital.

Most voters said that Khatami was committed to solving the country's problems although they were sceptical about how much room for manoeuvre he had as ultimate power remained with the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, backed by an equally arch-conservative Guardian Council and parliament.
"Inflation will come down, opportunities for young people will increase and social restrictions will be eased," said Abolfath, listening intently to his radio in his modest office.
But others thought the task facing Khatami when he replaces President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani would be difficult as he faced strong political and institutional opposition to reform.

"One year from here we will be disillusioned. They filtered the candidates in the first place to make sure they got who they wanted. It was an election between the bad and the worse," said Peyman, an 25-year-old office worker.
Nateq-Nouri's supporters were equally surprised by Khatami's victory and the size of the win.
"I voted for Nateq-Nouri because I thought he was pre- elected before because all the government figures voted for him. I am just amazed," said Jamshid, a fruit-juice seller.
